## College tuition

Researchers gathered data on the amount of money students paid to attend Elmhurst College in 2011. They collected information on 49 students, and for each student, we have:

* `family_income`: the student's family income (in 1000s of dollars)
* `price_paid`: the tuition price paid by the student (in 1000s of dollars)

Researchers believe that students with a higher family income will tend to pay more in tuition (as they will receive less financial aid).

### Choosing a model

Researchers consider a linear model on the original data, and also consider two different transformations of family income. Below are three sets of scatterplots, showing the original data and the two transformations, along with residual plots for the linear model with each set of variables.

```{r, include=F}

library(gridExtra)
```

```{r, echo=F, message=F, warning=F}
p1 <- elmhurst |>
  ggplot(aes(x = family_income, y = price_paid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se=F, method="lm") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Family income (1000s of $)",
       y = "Tuition paid (1000s of $)",
       title = "Original data")

m1 <- lm(price_paid ~ family_income, data = elmhurst)

p2 <- data.frame(x = predict(m1),
                 y = resid(m1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 0, intercept = 1, color="blue") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Predicted tuition paid (1000s of $)", 
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residual plot")

p3 <- elmhurst |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log(family_income), y = price_paid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se=F, method="lm") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "log(Family income)",
       y = "Tuition paid (1000s of $)",
       title = "Transformation 1")

m2 <- lm(price_paid ~ log(family_income), data = elmhurst)

p4 <- data.frame(x = predict(m2),
                 y = resid(m2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 0, intercept = 1, color="blue") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Predicted tuition paid (1000s of $)", 
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residual plot")

p5 <- elmhurst |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sqrt(family_income), y = price_paid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se=F, method="lm") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "sqrt(Family income)",
       y = "Tuition paid (1000s of $)",
       title = "Transformation 2")

m3 <- lm(price_paid ~ sqrt(family_income), data = elmhurst)

p6 <- data.frame(x = predict(m3),
                 y = resid(m3)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 0, intercept = 1, color="blue") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Predicted tuition paid (1000s of $)", 
       y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residual plot")

grid.arrange(p1, p3, p5, p2, p4, p6, ncol=3)
```


:::{.question}
#### Question 1

Based on the plots, write down a population regression model that allows the researchers to investigate their hypothesis. Explain your choice of model with reference to the plots.
:::

### Studentized residuals

One student has a family income of \$160,000 and paid \$10,200 in tuition. The standard deviation of the residuals (excluding this point) is $\widehat{\sigma}_\varepsilon = 4.76$.

:::{.question}
#### Question 7

Using the model chosen in question 1, compute the studentized residual for this student. 

Do you think we should be concerned about the influence of this point on the fitted line? Explain, with reference to both the studentized residual and the original data.
:::
